newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine polls set stage for presidential battle.
newsitem.headline: Philippine polls set stage for presidential battle.

text.p: About 25 million Filipinos vote in village polls nationwide on Monday, signalling the start of a political battle to choose President Fidel Ramos's successor.
In a nation where money and guns can spell victory or defeat for a candidate, police have been placed on full alert in 2,000 villages amid reports of intense political rivalries and vote buying.
At stake in the voting to be held in each of the Philippines' 42,000 villages -- known as barangay -- are the posts of village captain and seven councilmen.
Altogether, nearly half a million candidates are vying for 335,400 posts. Each barangay has an average population of 1,500.

Officially, the job of village officials is to keep the peace, flush out drug users, supervise responses to disasters, ensure garbage is collected and patch up quarrels among neighbours to keep them from clogging the courts.
Unofficially, they are the foot soldiers of powerful politicians and entrusted with bringing in votes during national elections, officials say.

"They are the grass-roots commanders of political parties. If we have political warlords, we also have fiefdoms at the barangay level," Commission on Elections executive director Resurreccion Borja told Reuters.
Borja said Monday's polls were vital to politicians aspiring to succeed Ramos in the May 1998 presidential elections because "the barangay leaders are the ones who will deliver the votes."
This is specially true in rural areas where most Filipinos live and which often are inaccessible to Manila politicians.
"That's why politicians are already pre-positioning themselves, building rural bailiwicks (power bases)," Borra said. "What we have now is a dry run for 1998."
At least a dozen politicians have already voiced interest in running for president, including three of Ramos's cabinet ministers and several congressmen and senators.
Ramos, himself, is barred by the constitution from running for a second term as president.

"Some politicians are giving away hundreds of thousands of pesos to some barangay leaders so that these people will be beholden to them," said Jose Concepcion, chairman of the National Movement for Free Elections (Namfrel), a citizens poll watchdog.
Concepcion, a former Philippine trade secretary, is himself running as barangay chief in Manila's Forbes Park district.

He is campaigning to keep the polls non-partisan. Meddling by politicians has corrupted the purpose for which barangays were set up, which was to serve everyone in the village regardless of political colour, he said.
The election code, in fact, bans parties and politicians from supporting barangay candidates. But in a political system that thrives on patronage the law is widely ignored.
Vote buying, which has bedevilled every Philippine election, is common. In poorer areas, votes are sought for 50 pesos ($1.90) each, residents say. In richer districts, the offer rises to 500 pesos.

"Barangay elections are supposed to be grassroots democracy in action, where families, neighbours will have a chance to run the affairs of their community. That's why we want to shield them from politics," Borja said.
"If we make the elections partisan, we destroy the village." ($1 = 26.3 pesos)
